query: Which material can be used for superconducting properties, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A refractory high‐entropy alloy (HEA) based on a MoNbTaW composition, when tuned by minor compositional adjustments, can exhibit superconductivity at cryogenic temperatures due to an enhancement of electron–phonon coupling arising from its disordered BCC lattice.
generation.material_initial_state: A nanocrystalline or polycrystalline refractory HEA containing Mo, Nb, Ta, and W processed via advanced methods (e.g., spark plasma sintering or LPBF) with a largely disordered BCC structure.
generation.intervention: Tuning the alloy composition (e.g., slight adjustments in the relative concentrations of Mo, Nb, Ta, and W) and employing combined experimental-simulation approaches (including scanning tunneling spectroscopy and first-principles electron–phonon coupling calculations).
generation.conditions: Measurements under cryogenic conditions (temperatures in the range of liquid helium temperatures) and controlled magnetic fields to identify superconducting transitions and critical parameters.
generation.structural_mediator: The high configurational entropy and intrinsic lattice distortions in the BCC phase of the HEA mediate modified electronic density of states and phonon spectra.
generation.mechanism: The disordered lattice promotes an enhanced electron–phonon coupling that facilitates electron pairing (Cooper pair formation), which is key to the onset of superconductivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The HEA is expected to exhibit a measurable superconducting transition (zero electrical resistance and Meissner effect) at a critical temperature comparable to or modestly lower than conventional superconductors, potentially with improved mechanical robustness.
generation.baseline: Conventional elemental superconductors (e.g., Nb or Ta) or binary superconducting alloys that require cryogenic cooling, serving as a performance benchmark.
generation.boundary: The superconducting properties may be sensitive to slight compositional inhomogeneities and processing-induced phase separations; if excessive disorder or phase decomposition occurs, the superconducting behavior might be suppressed.
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical temperature and superconducting gap remain uncertain due to the complex interplay between chemical disorder and electron–phonon interactions in HEAs, and further experimental validation is needed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of MoNbTaW-based HEA samples with systematic compositional variations. Cool each sample in a cryogenic setup while simultaneously measuring electrical resistance and magnetic susceptibility. Use scanning tunneling spectroscopy at various temperatures to monitor the emergence of superconducting gaps. Additionally, apply external magnetic fields to determine critical field strengths.
measurements: Temperature-dependent electrical resistance (search for zero-resistance state)
Magnetic susceptibility and Meissner effect measurements
Scanning tunneling spectroscopy to probe the superconducting gap
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If none of the samples, even after systematic composition tuning, exhibit a clear superconducting transition (i.e., zero resistance and Meissner effect) below the expected cryogenic temperatures or if the electron–phonon coupling does not improve with compositional adjustment, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications ( e.g . fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. The experimental and modeling results—showing a good agreement—can be applied to design and rapidly assess other alloys subjected to extreme environmental conditions. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Power stations

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are defined as equimolar or nonequimolar single- and multiphase solid solutions, depending on the number and type of principal/secondary metallic elements with the configurational entropy greater than 1.61 R , (where R is the gas constant) ( [1] , [2] ). The minimization of the Gibbs free energy by increasing the configurational entropy results in the formation of a single- or multiphase solid solution, such as body-centered cubic (BCC) ( [3] ), face-centered cubic (FCC) ( [4] ), and/or hexagonal close-packed solid-solution phases ( [5] ) instead of intermetallic compounds ( [6] ). Moreover, the random distribution of multiple elements with different atomic radii leads to a severely distorted lattice with variations in the interatomic distances along the crystallographic direction of the unit cells ( [3] ). These features, in turn, contribute to desirable mechanical properties, such as high hardness, strength, ductility, and softening resistance at room temperature (RT) and elevated temperatures ( [3] ).

decision.trend: Over the past several years, researchers have explored the design and processing of high‐entropy alloys (HEAs) and refractory alloy systems containing elements like Nb, Ta, Mo, and W – components that are well known from conventional superconductors. Early work was focused on improving mechanical performance, wear resistance, and thermal stability via advanced processing techniques (e.g., spark plasma sintering, LPBF). Later studies delved into dislocation dynamics and chemical short-range order in these alloys, yet the electronic properties, including superconductivity, were not systematically addressed. The common thread has been the use of complex, multi-principal element alloys to achieve robust microstructures while inadvertently including elements that are the basis for superconductivity. However, the studies have not yet pinpointed or explained the role that disorder and electron–phonon coupling play in enabling superconductivity in these HEA systems.
decision.unsolved: Despite the inclusion of superconducting elements (such as Nb and Ta) in many refractory HEAs, the detailed electron pairing mechanisms and the impact of chemical disorder on electron–phonon coupling remain unclear. There is a gap in connecting the microstructural stability and processing routes of these alloys to their potential superconducting behavior, including the optimization of critical temperature and magnetic field limits under feasible cryogenic conditions.
decision.lever: tuning the alloy composition (e.g., in a MoNbTaW-based HEA) and deploying advanced spectroscopic techniques (such as scanning tunneling spectroscopy) alongside first-principles electron–phonon coupling calculations
decision.why: This approach directly builds on the trend of using refractory HEAs that incorporate conventional superconducting elements while addressing the unsolved challenge of understanding and enhancing superconducting properties. By integrating targeted composition adjustments to optimize the electron–phonon interaction and using combined experimental-simulation efforts, researchers can elucidate the pairing mechanism and rationalize why a given material exhibits superconductivity under feasible conditions.
